name: Ancient Egyptian
place: The Nile valley, from the Delta to Nubia
blurb: The classical language of the pharaohs, spoken in the Middle Kingdom and carved on temples until Roman times.
facts: Egyptians called hieroglyphs mdw nṯr, 'the god's words'.
Hieroglyphs write no vowels, so 'Tutankhamun' is a modern way of saying twt-ꜥnḫ-jmn.
Champollion announced his decipherment in 1822, helped by the Greek text on the Rosetta Stone.
The last dated hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae in AD 394.
Egyptian lived on as Coptic, still heard in the services of the Coptic Church.

units.title: mdw nṯr
units.about: The first half of the hieroglyphic alphabet

guide.p: Hieroglyphs write consonants, never vowels. Egyptologists pronounce words by slipping in an e: nfr is 'nefer', nswt is 'nesut'.
The vulture ꜣ and the forearm ꜥ are consonants English lacks. Today both are simply said 'a': ꜥnḫ is 'ankh'.
The reed leaf j and the quail chick w are half-vowels, said 'i' and 'u' when a word needs a vowel.
Hieroglyphs run left to right, right to left, or down in columns. Read towards the faces of the people and animals.
ḥ is a strong h from the throat. ḫ is the ch of Scottish loch, ẖ the ch of German ich. š is 'sh'.
Egyptologists say the underlined letters like the ch of church and the j of judge.
The folded cloth 𓋴 and the door bolt 𓊃 were once different sounds, but by Middle Egyptian both are read s. This unit drills the cloth; you will meet the bolt in s 'man'.
Many signs write two or three consonants at once, and scribes add alphabet signs after them as a reading aid. In 𓋹𓈖𓐍 ꜥnḫ 'life', the ankh already says ꜥnḫ; n and ḫ just confirm it.
Determinatives end a word and are not read: 𓀀 for a man, 𓁐 for a woman. A stroke 𓏤 says the sign before it means what it shows.
Feminine nouns end in t, the bread loaf.
Put two nouns side by side and the second owns the first.
Possessives are endings joined with =. =j 'my' is written with the determinative 𓀀, =f 'his' with the viper.
ḥnꜥ, 'together with', is the usual way to join two nouns.

items.note: The pintail duck 𓅭 spells sꜣ by itself.

guide.p: An adjective comes after its noun and adds -t for a feminine noun.
Egyptians called their country kmt, 'the black land', after the dark Nile silt, and the desert dšrt, 'the red land'. The crossroads sign 𓊖 marks towns, and Egypt itself.
pr ꜥꜣ, 'the great house', was the palace. In the New Kingdom it came to mean the king himself, and reached English through Hebrew and Greek as 'pharaoh'.
hrw nfr, 'a good day', was a feast day. Banquet songs urge the guests to make one.

items.note: Also the sun god Ra.
In Egypt, the river was the Nile.

units.title: jnk
units.about: Say where things are and who people are

guide.p: A noun followed by a place already makes a sentence. jw at the start marks it as a statement and is not translated.
ex: the sun is in the sky

guide.p: After jw the pronoun is a suffix: =j I, =k you, =f he, =s she. On a noun the same endings mean my, your, his, her.
To say who someone is, start with jnk 'I' or ntk 'you', or end with pw 'this'.
Many Middle Kingdom people had a second, everyday name, their rn nfr or 'good name'.

items.note: Opens a statement. It has no tense and often no translation.
The sign is a face, ḥr.
Said to a man. To a woman: ntṯ.
Said to a man. To a woman: =ṯ.

units.title: ḥtp dj nswt
units.about: The offering formula and the titles of kings

guide.p: ḥtp dj nswt, 'an offering that the king gives', opens the prayer on countless Middle Kingdom stelae, false doors and coffins. It names a god, usually Osiris or Anubis, and asks for bread, beer, cattle and fowl for the ka, the life force, of the dead. Allen's Middle Egyptian and Gardiner's Egyptian Grammar both discuss it.

Words for the king and the gods are written first even when they are read later. ḥtp dj nswt is written nswt ḥtp dj (𓇓𓏏𓊵𓏙), mrj jmn is written jmn mrj. Such words share one tile here, joined by hyphens.
Stock phrases are often cut down to their key signs: ꜥnḫ wḏꜣ snb, said after a king's name, becomes 𓋹𓍑𓋴, and nṯr ꜥꜣ becomes 𓊹𓉻.
nṯr nfr 'the good god' and nb tꜣwj 'lord of the Two Lands', Upper and Lower Egypt, come before a king's name. dj ꜥnḫ 'given life' and mrj 'beloved of' a god come after it.

items.note: The sign is a loaf on a reed mat.
A form of rḏj 'to give'.
The dual of tꜣ 'land': Upper and Lower Egypt.
'The hidden one', god of Thebes.

units.title: sḏm.n=f
units.about: Say what happened: the past tense

guide.p: Put .n between the verb and its subject for something done: sḏm 'hear', sḏm.n=f 'he heard' or 'he has heard'. The n is the water ripple 𓈖, written straight after the verb.
Egyptian puts the verb first, then the subject, then the object, then everything else.
Verbs ending in j drop it in writing: prj 'go out' gives pr.n=j, jrj 'do' gives jr.n=j, gmj 'find' gives gm.n=j. mꜣꜣ 'see' usually loses its second ꜣ: mꜣ.n=f.
Egyptologists name every verb form after sḏm 'hear' with =f 'he'. 'The sḏm.n=f' means this past form of any verb.
n 'to, for' marks the person who receives something; r 'to, towards' marks where you go. After verbs of motion, m means 'from' as well as 'in'.
ex: I went out from my town

guide.p: Middle Kingdom officials filled their stelae with sḏm.n=f boasts such as pr.n=j m njwt=j and jr.n=j mꜣꜥt, 'I went out from my town … I did what is right'.

items.note: The ear 𓄔 spells sḏm by itself; the owl confirms the m.
The walking legs 𓂻 mark verbs of motion.
dj in the offering formula is a form of this verb.
The eye 𓁹 spells jr.
Also the goddess Maat, who keeps the world in order.

units.title: nfr sw
units.about: Describe people and states: adjectives, pronouns and the stative

guide.p: Put an adjective at the start and it becomes the statement: nfr sw 'he is good'. The subject follows it.
ex: he is happy (his heart is sweet)

guide.p: After an adjective, and as the object of a verb, pronouns take a short 'dependent' form: wj 'me', ṯw 'you', sw 'him, he', sj or st 'her, it'.
The stative, also called the pseudoparticiple, describes a state. It has its own endings: .kw 'I', .tj 'you' or 'she', and .w 'he', which is often not written. It usually follows jw and a subject.
With verbs of motion the stative means the journey is over.
An adjective can stand alone for a person: ḥqr 'a hungry man', ḥꜣy 'a naked man'. Officials boasted on their tomb walls of feeding and clothing them.
ex: I gave bread to the hungry

items.note: Said to a man. To a woman: ṯn.
The man with his hand to his mouth marks eating, speaking and feeling.
The double reed leaf 𓇋𓇋 is y.
Also 'priest', the man who keeps the temple pure.
The sparrow 𓅪 marks small, bad or weak things.

units.title: ḫꜣ m t ḥnqt
units.about: Count to a million and read the offering list

guide.p: Numbers are tallies. A stroke 𓏺 is 1, a cattle hobble 𓎆 is 10, a coil of rope 𓍢 is 100, a lotus 𓆼 is 1,000, a finger 𓂭 is 10,000, a tadpole 𓆐 is 100,000 and the god Heh 𓁨, arms raised, is a million. Repeat signs to add them up: 𓎆𓎆𓎆 is 30.
The number follows its noun, and the noun usually stays singular. Egyptologists often just write the digits: hrw 10.

Masculine plurals end in -w and feminine ones in -wt, written with three strokes 𓏥 or a sign drawn three times: 𓊹𓊹𓊹 nṯrw 'gods'. Pairs take the dual -wj or -tj, as in tꜣwj 'the Two Lands'. Adjectives agree.
A number can also come first, joined by m 'of'. The offering formula promises the dead ḫꜣ m t ḥnqt, 'a thousand of bread and beer'.
ex: a thousand of bread and beer

guide.p: Offering lists write each gift with one picture: 𓏐 a loaf, 𓏊 a beer jug, 𓃾 an ox head, 𓅿 a plucked bird.

items.note: As a numeral just a stroke 𓏺.

units.title: dj=f prt-ḫrw
units.about: Wish, promise and foretell: the sḏm=f and the future

guide.p: Verb plus suffix, with no .n, is the sḏm=f. At the start of a main clause it usually looks ahead: a wish, an urging or a promise. Context decides which.
ex: may he give an invocation offering

guide.p: After ḥtp dj nswt and the god's name comes dj=f prt-ḫrw, 'so that he may give an invocation offering': bread, beer, oxen and fowl, called up by the voice of a visitor for the ka of the dead.
jw, the subject, r 'towards' and the infinitive say what will happen.
ex: I will do what is right
he will go to the Residence

guide.p: The infinitive is the verb's name. Most verbs just use their stem, but verbs ending in j, and šmj, add t: jrj → jrt, rḏj → rḏjt, jj → jjt, prj → prt, šmj → šmt.
A dependent pronoun object jumps ahead of a noun subject.

Grammarians split the sḏm=f into several forms (perfective, imperfective, prospective) that are often spelled alike. In stories it can also tell the past, as in Sinuhe's ꜥr nṯr r ꜣḫt=f, 'the god ascended to his horizon'.

units.title: n sḏm=f
units.about: Say no, forbid and ask questions

guide.p: The arms 𓂜 negate a verb. n sḏm=f means 'he did not hear', but n sḏm.n=f means 'he does not hear' or 'he cannot hear'. The forms seem swapped, a famous puzzle of Egyptian grammar.
ex: he did not hear my voice

guide.p: nn before a noun says it does not exist; before a dependent pronoun and a place it says someone is not there.
ex: he is not in the house

guide.p: m before a verb forbids. It is a form of jmj, a verb meaning 'do not'.
jn at the start turns a statement into a yes-or-no question. Question words include nm 'who?' and jšst 'what?', often with pw 'it'.
In The Shipwrecked Sailor a giant snake roars at the castaway nm jn ṯw, 'who brought you?', three times before he can answer.
In Book of the Dead spell 125 the dead deny their sins one by one with n sḏm=f: n jr=j jsft, 'I have not done wrong'.

items.note: The sign is two arms held out empty.
Looks like m 'in', but stands before a verb.
rḫ means 'learn', so 'I have learned' is 'I know'.
The sign is a goose being plucked.
The opposite of mꜣꜥt.

units.title: sbꜣyt
units.about: Read the classics: wisdom, Sinuhe and the Book of the Dead

guide.p: A sbꜣyt, 'teaching', is advice from a wise father to his son. The Instruction of Ptahhotep, copied on the Middle Kingdom Papyrus Prisse, is the most famous. Its maxims use the negative command m and the bare verb as an order.
The imperative is simply the verb stem: ḏd 'speak!', jr 'do!'. That line comes from The Eloquent Peasant, who lectures a high official in nine speeches.
A verb can act as an adjective, 'who does': šms nb=f 'who follows his lord'. Sinuhe introduces himself this way.
ex: I was a follower who followed his lord

guide.p: The Story of Sinuhe is the masterpiece of Middle Egyptian prose. A courtier flees Egypt when King Amenemhat I dies, lives for decades in Syria, and is finally called home to be buried. It opens with his titles and sꜣ-nht ḏd=f, 'Sinuhe says'.

Its own title is rꜣw nw prt m hrw, 'spells for going out by day'. In spell 125 the dead stand before Osiris and 42 judges, greet the god with jw=j rḫ.kw ṯw rḫ.kw rn=k, 'I know you, I know your name', and swear jw=j wꜥb.kw, 'I am pure'.
When two nouns cannot sit side by side, n 'of' joins them. It agrees with the first noun: n after a masculine, nt after a feminine, nw after a plural.
ex: spells of going out by day
